rule: Triangle area is one-half the base times perpendicular height; irregular parcels can be split into nonoverlapping standard shapes and then added.
conditions: The supplied height must be perpendicular to the base and component areas must not overlap.
exceptions: A sloping side is not automatically the height, and omitting one-half doubles a triangle's area.

sources.locator: Printed page 559, Area of a triangle
sources.supports: Provides the half-base-times-altitude formula.

examples.summary: A triangle with a 120-foot base and an 80-foot perpendicular height contains 4,800 square feet, not 9,600.

rule: A use easement ordinarily burdens fee-owned land rather than removing its area from ownership; a price applied to all fee acreage uses the complete conveyed area.
conditions: The agreement prices all fee-owned land and supplies no separate easement discount or excepted fee strip.
exceptions: The easement can still reduce buildable area, utility, or market value; a true fee exception would change the conveyed area.

sources.locator: Printed pages 45-46, bundle of rights and appurtenances
sources.supports: Distinguishes property rights from physical land and easement benefits.
Supports the full-area calculation under the stated pricing assumption.

examples.summary: The 20-foot utility easement across the one-acre parcel may restrict building but does not ordinarily require deducting its strip from fee acreage.

rule: A project ordinarily must satisfy both valid public controls and enforceable private restrictions; approval from one authority does not cancel the other.
conditions: The stated restrictions are valid and no overriding statute or approved exception changes their application.
exceptions: Unenforceable or statutorily displaced private restrictions do not win merely by being stricter.

sources.supports: Authorizes local use, height, bulk, coverage, and setback regulation.
Addresses enforceable declaration restrictions and governing documents.

examples.summary: A building permit does not erase an enforceable covenant, and HOA approval does not excuse violation of a public requirement.

rule: Police power regulates land use for legitimate public purposes without necessarily acquiring the affected land.
conditions: The exercise describes a lawful public safety or land-use restriction, such as a setback.
exceptions: A regulatory loss in value alone is not proof of a compensable taking; constitutional taking questions require their own analysis.

sources.supports: Expressly authorizes establishment and maintenance of building setback lines.
Defines governmental regulation for public health, safety, and welfare.

examples.summary: The city requires a setback or correction of unsafe wiring without purchasing the occupied property.

rule: Eminent domain is the power to take private property for public use with required compensation, and condemnation is the acquisition process rather than an unsafe-building order.
conditions: Identify whether government is acquiring property or regulating a dangerous condition.
exceptions: Compensability and the lawful scope of acquisition depend on constitutional and statutory requirements.

sources.supports: Requires public use and just compensation for private property taken or damaged.
Distinguishes the taking power and its process from other governmental action.

examples.summary: Acquisition of a strip for transit differs from an order to correct unsafe wiring, although both may casually be called condemnation.

rule: Taxation and public special assessments impose lawful charges, while escheat concerns property without legally entitled successors; dying without a will is not automatically escheat.
conditions: Identify whether the government is levying a charge or receiving property after the applicable succession process.
exceptions: Ad valorem tax and benefit-related assessments need not share the same calculation base; intestate heirs can inherit without a will.

sources.locator: AD VALOREM, SPECIAL ASSESSMENT, and ESCHEAT
sources.supports: Defines value-based taxation, charges for public improvements, and reversion to the state when capable heirs are absent.

examples.summary: The four-notice comparison separates a public improvement assessment from the case with no legally entitled successor.

rule: The general plan sets coordinated long-term development policy; zoning specifies use and development standards, and construction requirements address the building itself.
conditions: Match the document to the policy, permitted land use, or construction-safety question being asked.
exceptions: A plan designation is not an individual permit, and a permitted use can still fail applicable building requirements.

sources.locator: Government Code section 65302, opening paragraph and subdivisions (a)-(h)
sources.supports: Requires development-policy text and diagrams plus specified elements, including environmental justice when applicable.
Authorizes detailed local use and development regulation.

sources.locator: Printed pages 465-468, General Plans and Zoning
sources.supports: Distinguishes coordinated development policy from zoning implementation.

examples.summary: A proposed use may satisfy zoning while its structure fails construction requirements; the reverse can also occur.

rule: Density, floor-area ratio, height, and building coverage measure distinct constraints; satisfying one numerical ceiling does not establish complete approval.
conditions: Use the exercise's density base and local definition of counted floor area.
exceptions: State-law overrides, bonuses, and other site constraints require separate consideration when applicable.

sources.supports: Authorizes building size, lot coverage, and land-use intensity controls.

examples.summary: Four units per acre on two acres gives eight units under that one rule, while 0.50 FAR on 20,000 square feet gives 10,000 square feet of counted floor area.

rule: A variance requires qualifying circumstances of the property and cannot authorize a use otherwise prohibited by the zone under Government Code section 65906.
conditions: Identify property-specific size, shape, topography, location, or surroundings and compare privileges in the same vicinity and zone.
exceptions: Financial preference alone is not the statutory basis, and a conditional use permit is a distinct authorization.

sources.supports: States the special-circumstances test, no-special-privilege condition, prohibited-use limit, and conditional-use distinction.

examples.summary: Unusual topography may justify dimensional relief, but calling a prohibited retail shop a profitable hardship does not create use-variance authority.

rule: A conditional use permit authorizes a use already contemplated conditionally in the zoning framework when required findings and conditions are satisfied.
conditions: The ordinance makes the proposed use conditionally available rather than outright prohibited.
exceptions: An application or supportive staff conversation is not an issued permit or general rezoning.

sources.supports: Explains specially authorized uses, spillover effects, and conditions that address compatibility.

examples.summary: The district may allow a facility only after review of traffic, operating hours, and neighborhood compatibility.

rule: A legal nonconforming use was lawful before the regulatory change; age alone does not legalize an originally prohibited use or guarantee rebuilding rights.
conditions: Establish lawful origin, continued status, and the governing jurisdiction's continuation limits.
exceptions: Expansion, abandonment, reconstruction, and termination rules vary by jurisdiction; the cited La Puente provision is a local example, not a statewide ordinance.

sources.supports: Defines lawful prior and continuing nonconformity and excludes unlawfully established uses, structures, and parcels.

examples.summary: A once-lawful workshop differs from an illegal use that has simply existed for years; fire does not guarantee unlimited reconstruction.

rule: A salesperson must distinguish an informal favorable response or pending application from an actual required development approval.
conditions: Determine which agency has authority and whether it has completed the required decision.
exceptions: A conceptual drawing or application does not establish that other separate permits or conditions are satisfied.

sources.supports: Authorizes discipline for substantial misrepresentation and specified false promises.

examples.summary: Calling staff encouragement an approved project materially changes the buyer's understanding of its risk and timeline.

rule: The Subdivision Map Act regulates physical divisions through local processes, while the DRE-administered Subdivided Lands Law regulates covered offerings and purchaser protection.
conditions: Check each law's definition, purpose, covered transaction, and exemptions rather than using one parcel-count rule for both.
exceptions: The general two-or-more division and five-or-more offering concepts do not decide every condominium, lease, or exempt transaction.

sources.supports: Defines subdivision for physical division, sale, lease, or financing and specified development categories.
Defines covered five-or-more subdivided lands with stated exclusions and preserves the Map Act's separate application.
Describes DRE's buyer-protection role for covered subdivision offerings.

examples.summary: The two laws can apply to the same proposed division for separate sales, and falling below five does not erase local division review.

rule: Map approval, DRE offering compliance, private architectural restrictions, and easement scope remain separate inquiries; a public report is material disclosure, not a blanket project approval.
conditions: The offering is covered by DRE requirements and the other stated restrictions remain legally applicable.
exceptions: A public report does not replace local approvals or guarantee construction quality, and lawful statutory overrides can affect private restrictions.

sources.supports: Identifies the physical division addressed by map regulation.
Identifies DRE-regulated offering categories.
Supports separately enforceable declaration and governing-document obligations.

sources.locator: Public Reports, purpose and required disclosures
sources.supports: Explains the report's information, disclosure, and offering function.

examples.summary: The six-unit project requires examination of local division, DRE offering, declaration, and easement constraints rather than a single approval stamp.

rule: For a nonexempt covered project, CEQA document choice follows the evidence: no significant-effect evidence supports a negative declaration; qualifying revisions may support a mitigated negative declaration; substantial evidence of possible significant effects requires an EIR.
conditions: For mitigation under section 21080(c)(2), the applicant makes or agrees to revisions before public release and the whole record leaves no substantial evidence of a significant effect in the revised project.
exceptions: CEQA exemptions and ministerial activities require separate analysis; a negative declaration does not mean project rejection or land-use approval.

sources.supports: States applicability, exemptions, revision timing, evidence standard, and the EIR route.

examples.summary: The chapter contrasts an ordinary negative declaration with pre-review revisions eliminating initially identified significant effects.

rule: Enforceable covenants can support judicial relief, including an injunction restraining prohibited work; paying damages and securing permission are not equivalent remedies.
conditions: Determine the restriction's enforceability and the party entitled to enforce it.
exceptions: A neighbor's apparent violation does not establish waiver or permission, and governing law can displace an otherwise stated restriction.

sources.supports: Provides enforcement of declarations and other governing documents, including prevailing-party fees.
Defines an injunction as a court writ or order requiring a person to refrain from an act.

examples.summary: The chapter contrasts an order stopping conduct with a damages award and rejects treating another owner's violation as automatic authorization.

rule: A functioning well or water source does not prove unlimited lawful extraction; reasonable beneficial use and applicable basin restrictions remain relevant.
conditions: Identify the legal basis of the right, authorized place and purpose of use, and applicable groundwater management.
exceptions: Overlying percolating groundwater and subterranean streams in known definite channels have different permit treatment.

sources.locator: What is a water right?; How do I know if I need a water right permit?
sources.supports: Distinguishes reasonable beneficial entitlement, overlying use, surface-water permits, and local groundwater restrictions.

sources.locator: SGMA framework and local groundwater sustainability agencies
sources.supports: Explains local management and sustainability plans for covered high- and medium-priority basins.

examples.summary: The buyer of the orchard must investigate the well and groundwater sustainability agency rather than accept unlimited pumping from land ownership.

rule: A qualifying riparian right generally allows reasonable use of natural flow on the connected riparian land, not export to a separate distant parcel or seasonal storage under that right alone.
conditions: Establish qualifying riparian land, natural flow, and the authorized place of use.
exceptions: Nonuse alone does not ordinarily extinguish riparian rights; imported water or releases from upstream storage are not natural-flow entitlement merely because they pass the parcel.

sources.supports: Explains natural flow, the connected parcel, drainage, storage limits, and nonuse.

examples.summary: The chapter contrasts reasonable use on the adjoining parcel with moving water to the same owner's distant property or storing wet-season flows.

rule: Appropriation is a distinct basis of water use, and new surface-water appropriations generally require State Water Board authorization rather than mere stream adjacency.
conditions: Identify the diversion, place of use, and date and scope of the claimed right.
exceptions: Valid pre-1914 appropriative rights require separate historical analysis; seniority does not permit waste or unreasonable use.

sources.locator: What is an appropriative water right?; Do I need a water right permit if I began using water before 1914?
sources.supports: Explains appropriation and the historical permit distinction, including changed or expanded uses.

examples.summary: The chapter contrasts a new surface-water appropriation with a claimed historical pre-1914 right instead of treating all diversions as riparian.

rule: Legal entitlement, pump capacity, and actual delivery are separate constraints; greater equipment capacity cannot cure a shortfall in authorized water.
conditions: Use the verified entitlement's volume and terms, then separately assess seasonal availability and infrastructure.
exceptions: Even a sufficient legal volume does not guarantee hydrologic supply or crop profitability.

sources.locator: What is a water right?; What are the benefits of water right laws?; What information and conditions will my water right permit contain?
sources.supports: Distinguishes permitted beneficial use, priority-related availability, and conditions on a water right.

examples.summary: A 60-acre-foot annual irrigation plan with only 45 authorized acre-feet needs 15 additional lawful acre-feet even if the pump can extract more.

rule: Natural gradual accretion or recession and sudden avulsion are different processes and can have different title consequences; artificial fill is not natural accretion.
conditions: Determine the pace, natural or artificial cause, type of water body, and governing boundary documents.
exceptions: Civil Code section 1014 preserves existing rights-of-way; public trust interests and other boundary rules remain relevant.

sources.supports: Addresses natural imperceptible formation on a river or stream bank and preserves existing rights-of-way.
Separately addresses sudden transport of a distinguishable bank portion.
Defines sudden perceptible loss or addition through water action.

sources.locator: What are Public Trust Lands?; Ownership and Use Issues
sources.supports: Explains public trust land and filled-waterway boundary disputes.

examples.summary: Gradual riverbank deposits, an overnight channel shift, and owner-imported shoreline fill cannot be treated as the same title event.

rule: Covered pre-1978 housing sales require prescribed lead information, known facts and available reports, and a buyer's inspection opportunity, not automatic seller remediation.
conditions: Confirm that the transaction and housing are covered and identify any lawful written change or waiver of the usual ten-day opportunity.
exceptions: Exempt transactions and housing require separate analysis; rental disclosure is not identical to the buyer's inspection opportunity.

sources.supports: Lists the pamphlet, known information, reports, warning, and the buyer's ten-day assessment or inspection opportunity.

examples.summary: The chapter separates disclosure of known lead hazards and available reports from a requirement to remove every painted surface before sale.

rule: Different building hazards require different evidence: asbestos condition and disturbance matter, radon cannot be ruled out by smell, and mold problems require attention to moisture.
conditions: Match the suspected hazard to competent investigation rather than a blanket visual safety assurance.
exceptions: Undisturbed intact asbestos material is not the same exposure situation as damaged or disturbed material; generic inspection does not establish absence of hidden hazards.

sources.locator: How to Identify Materials That May Contain Asbestos; What to Do If You Have Asbestos in Your Home
sources.supports: Explains limitations of visual identification and the importance of condition and disturbance.

sources.locator: Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas
sources.supports: States that radon cannot be seen or smelled and exposure requires testing.
Explains the need to control moisture and fix the water problem.

examples.summary: The chapter contrasts airborne-fiber risk, odorless radon, and a moisture problem underlying visible mold.

rule: Environmental due diligence distinguishes disclosure, records and site inquiry, targeted sampling, and conditional cleanup status; a generic home inspection is not commercial environmental clearance.
conditions: Use qualified investigation appropriate to the site's history, potential contaminants, and the scope of each report.
exceptions: A report may contain significant data gaps and limited sampling; no single observation proves every condition across the site.

sources.locator: What Are the Documentation Requirements for All Appropriate Inquiries?; Format for Reporting Results
sources.supports: Requires documented findings, data gaps, professional opinions, and distinguishes additional investigation and Phase II sampling.

examples.summary: The evidence table separates a seller's disclosure, historical site review, targeted sampling, and cleanup documentation for a former service station.

rule: CERCLA liability can be strict and retroactive and, where the harm is indivisible, joint and several; absence of negligence alone does not defeat a qualifying claim.
conditions: Establish the hazardous-substance release or threatened release, response costs, and a legally responsible party.
exceptions: Statutory defenses, protections, divisible harm, and special party circumstances can change the result.

sources.locator: Superfund Liability is; liability triggers; Types of Superfund Liable Parties
sources.supports: Identifies the three liability characteristics, triggering conditions, and categories of responsible parties.

examples.summary: The chapter explains why a responsible party may face more than an equal fraction of cleanup costs despite claiming it followed industry standards.

rule: A private environmental indemnity may allocate reimbursement between parties but does not itself transfer away CERCLA liability imposed against a responsible party.
conditions: Distinguish enforcement by government from contractual reimbursement between buyer and seller.
exceptions: A separate applicable statutory defense or governmental settlement must be established on its own terms.

sources.supports: Preserves private indemnification and subrogation while preventing transfer of the liability imposed by the section.

examples.summary: The buyer may retain contractual recourse against the seller while still facing a regulatory cleanup claim.

rule: Known contamination does not automatically defeat BFPP eligibility, but qualifying pre-acquisition inquiry and continuing statutory obligations are required.
conditions: Establish the applicable threshold criteria and take reasonable steps concerning continuing and threatened releases after acquisition.
exceptions: An inspection report or private indemnity is not complete immunity, and closing does not end compliance duties.

sources.supports: Allows acquisition with knowledge subject to requirements and identifies AAI and continuing reasonable steps.

examples.summary: The chapter contrasts a buyer who knows contamination exists with one who ignores a continuing release after closing.

rule: An Alquist-Priolo map addresses surface fault rupture, not every earthquake or natural hazard; being outside its zone is not an all-hazards clearance.
conditions: Identify which hazard and regulatory purpose the particular map addresses.
exceptions: Shaking, liquefaction, landslide, flood, fire, and site-specific conditions require relevant separate evidence.

sources.locator: Surface Fault Rupture Explained; Other Earthquake-Related Hazards
sources.supports: Distinguishes surface rupture from earthquakes without rupture and the separate seismic-hazard framework.

examples.summary: The chapter contrasts a mapped surface-rupture concern with the unsupported claim that an unmapped site has no shaking or other hazard risk.

rule: An active Williamson Act contract restricts agricultural or compatible use and binds successor owners; a purchase does not cancel it or establish subdivision entitlement.
conditions: Review the actual contract, permitted compatible uses, duration, and lawful termination procedures.
exceptions: A buyer's preference for housing development is not itself cancellation or nonrenewal, and local implementation varies.

sources.supports: Requires compatible-use limitations and binds successors.
Explains use restrictions in exchange for agricultural or open-space assessment treatment.

examples.summary: The orchard buyer discovers an active contract inconsistent with treating attractive farmland as immediately development-ready.

rule: A conservation easement can impose an enforceable conservation limitation on retained fee title and bind later owners without the public acquiring the fee.
conditions: Identify the instrument's conservation purpose and restrictions on the particular land.
exceptions: The owner can retain title while losing some development choices; it is not an ordinary temporary revocable permission.

sources.supports: Defines an instrument imposing conservation limitations binding successive owners.

examples.summary: The rural owner retains title subject to an open-space conservation restriction rather than conveying the entire parcel to the county.

rule: Coastal development authority and public trust rights are distinct constraints that can remain relevant to redevelopment of a privately marketed waterfront site.
conditions: Check the proposed activity, coastal jurisdiction, certified local program, title boundaries, and public trust interests.
exceptions: A prior house or a waterfront deed does not automatically authorize reconstruction or exclusion of all public shoreline use.

sources.supports: Explains coastal regulation, broad development activity, and shared state-local responsibilities.

sources.locator: What are Public Trust Lands?; Ownership and Use Issues
sources.supports: Explains sovereign lands, filled areas, and continuing public trust rights.

examples.summary: The buyer replacing a coastal house must assess the new work and public access rather than infer permission from the old building.

rule: Reservation or other publicly associated land may involve trust title, leasehold, permits, and distinct authority; acquiring improvements does not itself establish fee ownership of the underlying land.
conditions: Read the actual land status and the precise interest offered rather than importing assumptions from an ordinary private fee sale.
exceptions: Federal Indian reservations and individual parcels have particular histories and statuses; not every parcel with tribal associations has identical title.

sources.locator: Answer, What is a federal Indian reservation?
sources.supports: Explains tribal homelands and federal trust title on behalf of the tribe.

examples.summary: The chapter distinguishes buying improvements on leased land from acquiring fee title to the underlying site.
